headline: Africa sells its carbon at $3 a tonne. The same tonne is worth up to sixty times more once it leaves the continent.
standfirst: Africa owns the forest, yet it is others who set the price of its carbon. The continent holds some of the largest carbon sinks on earth, and a fast-growing market now pays it to keep them standing, but the price that market pays is set elsewhere. The African Development Bank's own former president has said foreign buyers sometimes pay as little as three dollars a tonne for African carbon, while a comparable permit in Europe's regulated market can cost around two hundred. He called it a carbon grab. Read through the Corridor Index and the economic-sovereignty question: who prices Africa's natural capital, and who captures the value once the credit leaves the continent.

headline: African pension funds are buying the continent's hotels. Five foreign brands keep 80 percent of the control.
standfirst: African Capital, Foreign Control. Africa's hotel-development pipeline stands at a record 123,846 rooms across 675 projects, and five foreign groups — Marriott, Hilton, Accor, IHG and Radisson — hold roughly 80 percent of it. Increasingly the money is African, with pension funds in South Africa, Zambia and Tanzania taking lead ownership of the buildings. But owning the freehold is not controlling the asset: under the standard management contract the brand takes a fee on revenue, a fee on profit, mandatory brand-standard procurement and reservation-system charges, across a 20-to-30-year term the owner cannot cheaply escape. Read through the Corridor Index: the ownership-control gap, and why owning the building is not capturing its value.

headline: Booking.com can't stop a French hotel undercutting it. It can still stop a Kenyan one.
standfirst: When a foreign visitor books an African lodge through an international online travel agency, 15 to 30 percent of what they pay leaves the continent as commission before they arrive. The deeper leak is the one the operator cannot escape: the platform's contract has historically barred the property from contacting the guest directly, from taking payment directly, and from offering a lower price on its own website, so the operator can never convert that guest into a direct customer and never stop paying the commission. In 2024 the European Union banned these clauses and named Booking.com a gatekeeper; African operators sign the same contracts with no such protection. Read through the Corridor Index: enforced disintermediation, the digital layer of tourism value capture.

headline: Every African state protects its national carrier. Together they have built one of the world's most expensive skies.
standfirst: Libreville and Bangui are about 1,000 kilometres apart; the flight between them takes at least nine hours, requires a change of plane, and costs around $1,000, while Paris to Madrid costs a fifth as much. Africa agreed to a single air market in 2018, the Single African Air Transport Market, and eight years on 38 states have signed and 26 have committed to implement it, yet only about a fifth of African air traffic is intra-continental and fewer than one in five intra-African routes has a direct flight. Read through the Corridor Index: a coordination failure in which every state protects its national carrier and the continent taxes the tourism it says it wants.

headline: When the borders closed in 2020, South Africa's foreign tourism revenue fell 69 percent. The market that held was a nation visiting itself.

headline: When sovereign wealth buys the coast: Gulf capital, African tourism and the new geography of strategic ownership.

headline: Africa's largest tourism market already exists. Our foreign-exchange metrics can't see it.
standfirst: Roughly four in five of the world's tourists travel within their own region. In Africa the official figure is far lower, and the gap is treated as a market not yet built. The opposite is true: the market exists at scale, and it is the measurement that has not been built. Africa's largest body of travellers are its own people crossing its own borders to trade and visit family, spending in local currency through informal channels the tourism statistics were never designed to count. Read through the Corridor Index framework: the market you price in dollars is the only market you measure, and it is not the biggest one.

headline: Four African countries have ratified the continent's free-movement protocol in seven years. The trade deal moves goods faster than the continent moves people.

Seven years on, the trade area is operational and the free-movement protocol has four ratifications, the most recent in July 2019. Read through the Sovereign Tourism Architecture framework: the announcement is not the policy, and the execution is the whole of it.
